title: Algebraic Simplifier does not transform `Concat(X,X)`
author: jaiarora0011
body: The algebraic simplifier contains a rewrite implemented in HandleConcat, which transforms a concatenation of the same operand along a degenerate dimension, to a broadcast of reshape. As an example, the following program ENTRY main {   x = s8[2,1,4] parameter(0)   ROOT concat.res = s8[2,5,4] concatenate(x, x, x, x, x), dimensions={1} }  is transformed to ENTRY main {   x = s8[2,1,4] parameter(0)   reshape.1 = s8[2,4] reshape(x)   ROOT bcast.res = s8[2,5,4] broadcast(reshape.1), dimensions={0,2} }  However, the simplifier fails to do the transformation if the concatenation is binary, i.e., the following program is not transformed: ENTRY main {   x = s8[3,1,4] parameter(0)   ROOT concat.res = s8[3,2,4] concatenate(x, x), dimensions={1} }  The culprit for this is the rewrite implement just before that, which transforms a binary concat with a broadcasted scalar as an operand into a pad:                xla/xla/hlo/transforms/simplifiers/algebraic_simplifier.cc                   Lines 1903 to 1911       in       33ec822                                                 if (operands.size() == 2) {                                             // A binary concat with a broadcasted scalar as an operand can be converted                                             // into a pad which is simpler to fold into other operations.                                             bool is_effective_low_pad = Match(                                                 operands[0], m::Broadcast(m::Op().WithShape(m::Shape().IsScalar())));                                             bool is_effective_high_pad = Match(                                                 operands[1], m::Broadcast(m::Op().WithShape(m::Shape().IsScalar())));                                             if (!is_effective_low_pad && !is_effective_high_pad) {                                               return absl::OkStatus();                     On line 1910, it prematurely returns if the binary concat is not an effective low or high scalar padding. I have implemented a simple fix with a unit test in e5d9e30.

title: XLA duplicates input arguments memory because of wrapped_transpose
author: qGentry
body: Hi, I have simple LLM training step that computes forward+backward pass and updates weights. It is LoRA training, so only very small subset of parameters is trainable (70B total parameters, ~600M trainable). I've checked memory analysis and found that actual memory consumption is way bigger than expected and figured out that this is because XLA is doing some very weird transposition of input weights, resulting in effectively doubling of memory usage for 70B model parameters. Can I somehow disabled this optimization or overcome this issue in some other way? I've tested it on both JAX 0.4.34 and latest version (JAX 0.6.1) Here's attached HLO dump: hlo.tgz Some of the transposed buffer names: wrapped_transpose.5 input_transpose_fusion.3 wrapped_transpose.10

title: [TPU] Bug: TPU X64 rewriting issue on c64
author: bjenik
body: I am getting the following error somewhere deep in a fairly large jit on TPU: jaxlib._jax.XlaRuntimeError: UNIMPLEMENTED: While rewriting computation to not contain X64 element types, XLA encountered an HLO for which this rewriting is not implemented: %all-reduce.0 = c64[16,...]{0,...} all-reduce(%transpose.18), channel_id=1, replica_groups={...}, use_global_device_ids=true, to_apply=%region_21.4425, metadata={...}  I am unfortunately not able to create a shareable minimal example - the compiler gets rid of the all-reduce over c64 in all of my smaller attempts, and spilts it into all-reduce over the equivalent fp32. I am not certain if the issue at hand is that it should have also dealt with  the c64 in my larger jit but doesn't, or if the c64 is getting misclassified and shouldn't be targeted by the X64 rewriting in the first place because it actually is 2 fp32, or if the rewriting needs to be expanded to support all-reduce.

title: Horizontal loop fusion can increase memory consumption by order of magnitude
author: jaro-sevcik
body: Here is a JAX repro (tested on GH200 GPU, but should repro on any GPU with 40-120GB), it reproduces with ToT JAX. import jax import jax.numpy as jnp  SIZE=40000 OUTER=16  @jax.jit def f(x):     for i in range(OUTER):       x, large_temp = jax.lax.scan(lambda acc, y: (acc + y, acc + y), x, jnp.ones(SIZE))       x += jnp.sum(large_temp, axis=-1)     return x  x = jnp.ones(SIZE)  compiled_f = f.lower(x).compile() print(compiled_f.memory_analysis()) f(x) With export XLA_FLAGS=, this runs out of memory trying to allocate ~100GB and reports: 2025-05-13 09:18:45.074199: W external/xla/xla/hlo/transforms/simplifiers/hlo_rematerialization.cc:3021] Can't reduce memory use below 67.69GiB (72678595712 bytes) by rematerialization; only reduced to 95.40GiB (102432320060 bytes), down from 95.40GiB (102432320060 bytes) originally 2025-05-13 09:18:55.172253: W external/xla/xla/tsl/framework/bfc_allocator.cc:501] Allocator (GPU_0_bfc) ran out of memory trying to allocate 95.40GiB (rounded to 102432004352)requested by op 2025-05-13 09:18:55.172300: W external/xla/xla/tsl/framework/bfc_allocator.cc:512] *___________________________________________________________________________________________________ E0513 09:18:55.172311 1808266 pjrt_stream_executor_client.cc:2908] Execution of replica 0 failed: RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED: Out of memory while trying to allocate 102432004240 bytes. [tf-allocator-allocation-error=''] Traceback (most recent call last):   File "/opt/host/horizontal-oom/example.py", line 18, in <module> CompiledMemoryStats(generated_code_size_in_bytes=18364, argument_size_in_bytes=160000, output_size_in_bytes=160000, alias_size_in_bytes=0, temp_size_in_bytes=102432004240, host_generated_code_size_in_bytes=0, host_argument_size_in_bytes=0, host_output_size_in_bytes=0, host_alias_size_in_bytes=0, host_temp_size_in_bytes=0)     f(x) jaxlib._jax.XlaRuntimeError: RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED: Out of memory while trying to allocate 102432004240 bytes. -------------------- For simplicity, JAX has removed its internal frames from the traceback of the following exception. Set JAX_TRACEBACK_FILTERING=off to include these.  With export XLA_FLAGS="--xla_disable_hlo_passes=horizontal-loop-fusion-for-copy", the program runs fine, using ~13GB: CompiledMemoryStats(generated_code_size_in_bytes=17348, argument_size_in_bytes=160000, output_size_in_bytes=160000, alias_size_in_bytes=0, temp_size_in_bytes=12832004008, host_generated_code_size_in_bytes=0, host_argument_size_in_bytes=0, host_output_size_in_bytes=0, host_alias_size_in_bytes=0, host_temp_size_in_bytes=0)  It is worth noting that even 13GB is 2x more than should be needed - it looks like XLA likes to keep around an initialized 6GB constant zero array so that it can produce initialized output buffer for the scan by just copying.

title: [XLA:GPU] Bad predication in transpose emitter
author: jreiffers
body: #26103 relaxed triggering for the transpose emitter. Unfortunately, it appears that the cost model is no longer aligned with the real performance of these fusions, in particular when there is a large prologue. Here is an example test case: TEST_F(PriorityFusionTest, Pr26103Regression) {   auto module = *ParseAndReturnVerifiedModule(R"( HloModule module  %region_1.34 (Arg_0.31: f32[], Arg_1.32: f32[]) -> f32[] {   %Arg_0.31 = f32[] parameter(0)   %Arg_1.32 = f32[] parameter(1)   ROOT %add.33.0 = f32[] add(%Arg_0.31, %Arg_1.32) }  %fused_computation (param_0.31: f32[1,4,8192,8192,4]) -> f32[4,64,8192,4] {   %param_0.31 = f32[1,4,8192,8192,4]{4,3,2,1,0} parameter(0)   %bitcast.49.1 = f32[4,64,128,8192,4]{4,3,2,1,0} bitcast(%param_0.31)   %constant.8.2 = f32[] constant(0)   ROOT %reduce.5.1 = f32[4,64,8192,4]{3,2,1,0} reduce(%bitcast.49.1, %constant.8.2), dimensions={2}, to_apply=%region_1.34 }  %fused_computation.2 (param_0.27: f32[1,4,8192,8192,4], param_1.21: f32[4,8192,4]) -> bf16[32768,4,8192] {   %param_0.27 = f32[1,4,8192,8192,4]{4,3,2,1,0} parameter(0)   %param_1.21 = f32[4,8192,4]{2,1,0} parameter(1)   %broadcast.4.3 = f32[1,4,8192,8192,4]{4,3,2,1,0} broadcast(%param_1.21), dimensions={1,3,4}   %divide.4 = f32[1,4,8192,8192,4]{4,3,2,1,0} divide(%param_0.27, %broadcast.4.3)   %convert.1.3 = bf16[1,4,8192,8192,4]{4,3,2,1,0} convert(%divide.4)   %bitcast.41.1 = bf16[32768,8192,4]{2,1,0} bitcast(%convert.1.3)   ROOT %transpose.11.1 = bf16[32768,4,8192]{2,1,0} transpose(%bitcast.41.1), dimensions={0,2,1} }  %fused_computation.8 (param_0.22: parameter(0)   %param_2.11 = bf16[4,8192,32768]{2,1,0} parameter(2)   %convert.0.8 = f32[4,8192,32768]{2,1,0} convert(%param_2.11)   %constant.6.1 = f32[] constant(0.0883)   %broadcast.2.1 = f32[4,8192,32768]{2,1,0} broadcast(%constant.6.1), dimensions={}   %multiply.0.7 = f32[4,8192,32768]{2,1,0} multiply(%convert.0.8, %broadcast.2.1)   %bitcast.3.5 = f32[1,4,8192,8192,4]{4,3,2,1,0} bitcast(%multiply.0.7)   %param_1.16 = f32[1,4,8192,8192,4]{4,3,2,1,0} parameter(1)   %select.0.5 = f32[1,4,8192,8192,4]{4,3,2,1,0} select(%param_0.22, %bitcast.3.5, %param_1.16)   %param_3.13 = %subtract.28.3 = f32[1,4,8192,8192,4]{4,3,2,1,0} subtract(%select.0.5, %broadcast.27.3)   ROOT %exponential.0.1 = f32[1,4,8192,8192,4]{4,3,2,1,0} exponential(%subtract.28.3) }  %fused_computation.11 title: Fix issues with ARM build after latest hermetic changes
author: dimvar
body: After commit 3d5ece6, some XLA targets such as //xla/stream_executor/cuda:cub_sort_kernel_cuda_impl_f32_b64 started failing on ARM with the error: clang: error: unknown argument: '-Xcuda-fatbinary=--compress-all' clang: error: unknown argument: '-nvcc_options=expt-relaxed-constexpr' clang: warning: CUDA version is newer than the latest supported version 12.3 [-Wunknown-cuda-version]  The problem is that XLA is passing nvcc-only options to clang. I've discussed these already with Yurii and Yulia on chat, but filing to track.

title: Possibility to specify strides when sending the data from buffer to host
author: sebffischer
body: When creating a PJRT Buffer from data that is in column-major format, the byte_strides argument can be used to handle the conversion                xla/xla/pjrt/pjrt_c_api_client.h                    Line 338       in       6d9fe38                                                 std::optional<absl::Span<int64_t const>> byte_strides,                     However, this is not generally possible when moving the data back to the host. In principle, this seems to be possible with the host_layout field here but this does not work in general, because not all plugins support this. Would it be possible to add a byte_strides field also when sending the data back?

title: Why does tfrt use only one stream for gpu client?
author: skewer
body: I am working the SDK of a gpu-like device, and  I am learning the runtime design of XLA, including PJRT, IFRT and TFRT. As explained in #15168, tfrt_gpu is a new PJRT implementation for GPU. I have two questions about this design as I read the code:  why is a new gpu client needed other than se_gpu_pjrt_client in XLA? All works including h2d, d2h memory copys and kernel works are submitted to the only stream std::unique_ptr<se::Stream> stream_ in the class TfrtGpuDevice. According to nvidia's document about cuda stream, these works will be processed by gpu in serial, missing the opportunity to overlap memory copy and computation. What's the consideration here?  Thank you!

title: Passing Kernels to FFI
author: dbs4261
body: Hi folks, I've been looking at wrapping some ray tracing code for use in JAX. Lets just ignore that ray traversal is not differentiable; that isn't relevant to what I want to do. My understanding of the normal XLA FFI use, is that is provides the information to just launch a CUDA kernel on a given stream. So one of my calls could essentially be optixLaunch(...), and that would force the synchronization of all tensors going in and out of it. But that's not what I am having a hard time wrapping my head around. The issue is more that I would like to use XLA/JAX to generate the modules in the shader binding table. So when optixLaunch(...) gets traced it would then lower the kernels to PTX either AOT or JITed. Would this even be possible within the constraints of how XLA works?

title: GPU mocking hangs the compiler (in autotuning)
author: jaro-sevcik
body: When we use GPU mocking to mock multiple processes, the autotuner sharding will try to get autotuning results from the mock processes. That will hang. JAX repro: import jax import jax.numpy as jnp from jax.sharding import Mesh, PartitionSpec as P, NamedSharding import numpy as np  jax.config.update("jax_mock_gpu_topology", "4x8x1")  print(jax.devices())  devices = np.array(jax.devices()).reshape(4, 4, 2) mesh = Mesh(devices, ('x', 'y', 'z')) NS = lambda *s: NamedSharding(mesh, P(*s)) DP = lambda a, s: jax.device_put(a, NS(*s))  @jax.jit def mm(x, y):   return jnp.dot(x, y)  x = DP(jnp.ones((16, 16)), ('x', 'z')) y = DP(jnp.ones((16, 16)), ('y', None))  # This hangs in the compiler's autotuner. out = mm(x, y) print(out.sharding)

title: [Proposal] Extract the Profiling Subsystem into a Dedicated OpenXLA Repository
author: blitzerr
body: Motivation The XLA profiling subsystem, currently located under xla/third_party/tsl/profiler, is a powerful and well-designed component. It is generic, modular, and extensible, making it valuable not just for XLA, but potentially for the broader ML ecosystem. The core concepts, including TraceMe, TraceMeRecorder, ProfilerSession, and the XPlane utilities, provide a robust foundation for host and device tracing. However, because they are deeply embedded within the XLA monorepo, it is difficult for other projects to consume them without depending on all of XLA. I propose that we extract the profiling subsystem into its own repository within the OpenXLA organization, similar to openxla/stablehlo or openxla/shardy. This would create a focused repository for high-performance C++ tracing infrastructure. Next Steps This is a significant architectural change, and I wanted to bring it up for discussion with the community and maintainers. If there is consensus that this is a valuable direction, I am happy to help with the work required to submit PRs for this migration. Thank you for your consideration!

title: jax.debug.print statement support for PJRT devices
author: tapspatel
body: When jit compiling graphs from jax that have jax.debug.print(), the following stablehlo custom call gets inserted into the graph stablehlo.custom_call @xla_ffi_python_cpu_callback  However, this pass is not available in PJRT devices due to PJRT not linking against openxla (see "Toolchain Independent" from https://opensource.googleblog.com/2023/05/pjrt-simplifying-ml-hardware-and-framework-integration.html). jax.debug.print() is extremely useful for any model developer, and it would be extremely beneficial to have this enabled for PJRT devices.

title: Regression in fusion behavior on GPU

title: Loop optimization
author: wjr-z
body: For example, I need to use partial prefix sum, that's : $$output[x, y] = \sum_{i=x-k+1}^{x} input[x, y]$$ When k is large, it's bad to use ReduceWindow, because its complexity will be O(N * k) (N is total size) A better solution is to use a sliding window. To do this, i have to use While, DynamicSlice and DynamiceUpdateSlice.  In this case, maybe a EmptyOp is needed, even every line will be filled by DynamiceUpdateSlice, but generated IR shows the Broadcast (used for zero initialized) won't be remove. Parallel of WhileOp maybe is feasible? At least for simple iterators, such as simple range loops, may it be achievable? I haven't specifically studied GPU backend, and it's possible that what I said is incorrect. However, this may introduce the issue of nested parallelism.

author: wenboqian
body: Description When using jax.profiler, I found that if I set os.environ['XLA_FLAGS'] = '--xla_hlo_profile=true', it will raise error below:  I am trying to profile the duration of fine-grained HLO operations, e.g. add.3.3 in a GPT2 model on GPU using jax.profiler. %fused_add.1 {   ...   %add.3.3 = f32[256,768]{1,0} ...}   ... } %command_buffer {   ...   %loop_add_fusion.1 = ..., calls=%fused_add.1   ... } ENTRY %main.332 {   ... Is it possible to get the duration for each fine-grained HLO operation in JAX? Or is this not achievable on GPU due to asynchronous parallel execution, which only provides the execution duration of the wrapped fusion HLO op? title: Synchronous Python callbacks from non-calling thread
author: kcdodd
body: This issue is to report a possible regression from #21980, where callbacks were changed to execute synchronously to avoid depleting the thread pool and causing a deadlock. For a while after that change it appeared that all callbacks would run within the same thread that launched the computation, but recently I've noticed callbacks sometimes run in a different thread. It seems that the logic in PjRtLoadedExecutable still sets and respects kSynchronous, and even though ThunkExecutor chooses "sequential" execution, at any point a dependency that is not immediately ready will stage out the remaining work (the callback) in an async event. The main thread runs ahead back to the executable where it blocks until the thunk completes. I'm pretty ignorant of how threads are managed in this case, but it seems the main thread basically is suspended until the computation finishes (waiting at the block until ready). Each time a callback is staged out that thread becomes unavailable for work and multiple callbacks can still deadlock. There are other reasons that it would be preferable to have callbacks always happen in the calling thread, but that has more to do with interacting with non-jax/xla code from the callback itself.

title: Support and Behavior of JIT Compilation for Dynamic Shapes in XLA
author: diligentliu
body: Hi, I have a question regarding dynamic shape support in TensorFlow + XLA. When I use tf.function(jit_compile=True) with TensorSpecs that have partially unknown dimensions (e.g., [None, 4096]), I noticed that XLA seems to generate the corresponding compiled kernel at runtime based on the actual input shapes. From my understanding, for dynamic shapes, XLA does not precompile a fully general kernel. Instead, it relies on just-in-time (JIT) compilation to produce a concrete CUDA kernel once it receives concrete input shapes. This appears to be different from frameworks like TVM, where the graph is first optimized statically and then executed; in TVM, optimizations can be applied based on known static shapes before runtime execution, potentially enabling more aggressive operator fusion and memory planning. Could you please confirm if my understanding is correct? Specifically:   Is dynamic shape support in XLA primarily implemented via this runtime JIT compilation approach?   Is there any ongoing effort or recommended approach to allow more static-graph-like optimizations for partially dynamic shapes, similar to how TVM can optimize a graph based on partially known shapes before execution?   I am particularly interested in understanding whether XLA has mechanisms to reduce runtime compilation overhead for workloads with dynamic batch sizes or other partially unknown dimensions.

title: Verifier failure on collective permute with mixed floating point precision (on multi-GPU)
author: jaro-sevcik
body: If collective permutes of mixed precisions get combined, the verifier will fail on the resulting code. title: Configure layout assignment for transposes
author: xrennvidia
body: By default, layout assignment tries to assign a layout to transposes that make them a bitcast. This layout is then propagated inside the HloComputation, which means if it does not cancel out with another transpose, there may be a copy op in some other part of the computation. This copy will later be turned back into a transpose. In T5X, we observed that default XLA layout assignment gives us many transposes in each transformer layer, which results in perf overheads. We tried to fix this problem by manually transposing T5X network input, however, the manually inserted transpose was ignored by XLA, which also creates many transposes in each layer. @akuegel created a PR #1485 which can stop our manually inserted transpose from being ignored. It turns out that this flag really can help us get better perf. I built a unit test with one T5X encoder layer, default runtime without manual transpose is 11.02ms. Runtime with manual transpose but without Adrian's PR is 11.04ms. After I apply both manual transpose and Adrian's PR (XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_transpose_to_bitcast=false), runtime becomes 10.63ms. Clearly, Adrian's PR is helpful. BTW, you can find my unit test HLO from here https://drive.google.com/drive/u/1/folders/1MRsPJqF7M-DoFRT3Gw8kYKHSoPAKPDUi Unfortunately, Adrian told us that his PR cannot be merged because it's controversial and would restricts what they can do in compiler. To get better perf, I file this github issue to discuss what other possible solutions that we can have. One suggested solution is to use a no-op custom call as "barrier" so that transposes do not get propagated. However, we still do not know how to do this easily without affecting performance. Other ideas that have been proposed is allowing a metadata annotation for the transpose. We do not have a concrete solution yet, I hope we can nail down this problem by discussing here. Thanks a lot.

title: glibc malloc: process could monopolise host memory when compiling
author: v01dXYZ
body: Context After compiling a deep and large computation graph, the process monopolises a large amount of memory (more than 2.5GB). This problem is encountered with jax==0.4.6, xla from tensorflow repo (43e9d313548ded301fa54f25a4192d3bcb123330). It could be damaging when the process is long-running. Cause With the glibc allocator, allocation of small objects (malloc(size) with size<=1032) could make the process never return a large portion of the heap memory to the system. Two simple cases that generate this behaviour:  Case 0: allocation of lot of small objects Case 1: a small object is allocated with the heap size increasing, then this object is quickly deallocated  Case 0 {     std::vector<std::vector<char>> v(1 << 20, std::vector<char>(1032, 0)); } Case 1 {     // we use a variable to ensure the deallocation occurs only at end of scope     std::vector<char> o(1032 + 1, 0);     std::vector<std::vector<char>> v(1 << 20, o);     {         std::vector<char> tmp(1032, 0);     }  } Possible solutions One solution is to invoke malloc_trim(...), but this is not portable. Another one is to use an alternative allocator (jemalloc 5.3.0 does not exhibit the faulty behaviour). Finally, I tried to set a maximum size to the data segment, unfortunately malloc turns unusable if only this option is configured (maybe there are env variables for malloc to configure too). Remarks  this behaviour is present b/c glibc is built by default with tcache enabled (tested with version: 2.37 and version: 2.31 on a x86_64 linux machine). It is because when deallocating a small object, the chunk is put in the tcache if there are available slots, thus preventing consolidation. with XLA_FLAG="--xla_cpu_use_xla_runtime", the following line generates heap memory distention when compiling a large and deep computation graph: service/copy_insertion.cc#L2176

title: Questions about VectorLoad in LLVM IR dumped by XLA

body: Hi, recently, I'm trying to analyze the performance of softmax with openXLA. When comparing two LLVM IRs, I found that certain LLVM passes have converted scalar load to vector load as shown below. ir-no-opt.ll %37 = getelementptr inbounds half, ptr %arg2, i32 %linear_index1   %38 = load half, ptr %37, align 2, !invariant.load !11  ir-with-opt.ll  %arg37 = addrspacecast ptr %arg3 to ptr addrspace(1)   %arg25 = addrspacecast ptr %arg2 to ptr addrspace(1)   %arg13 = addrspacecast ptr %arg1 to ptr addrspace(1)   %arg01 = addrspacecast ptr %arg0 to ptr addrspace(1)   %0 = tail call i32 @llvm.nvvm.read.ptx.sreg.ctaid.x(), !range !8   %1 = shl nuw nsw i32 %0, 10   %2 = tail call i32 @llvm.nvvm.read.ptx.sreg.tid.x(), !range !9   %3 = shl nuw nsw i32 %2, 2   %linear_index_base = or i32 %1, %3   %4 = lshr i32 %0, 2   %5 = zext i32 %linear_index_base to i64   %6 = getelementptr half, ptr addrspace(1) %arg25, i64 %5   %7 = load <4 x half>, ptr addrspace(1) %6, align 8, !invariant.load !10   %8 = extractelement <4 x half> %7, i32 0   %9 = extractelement <4 x half> %7, i32 1   %10 = extractelement <4 x half> %7, i32 2   %11 = extractelement <4 x half> %7, i32 3  Question: Which LLVM passes did this work? by the way, I have tried to dump all LLVM passes by setting export XLA_FLAGS="--xla_gpu_dump_llvmir" ， but didn't find any useful cues. Any cues or ideas would be highly appreciated. Thanks.

title: Batched TriangularSolve of singular matrix returns incorrect results
author: jakevdp
body: Here's a short repro in JAX, that more or less passes the inputs directly to TriangularSolveOp: import jax import jax.numpy as jnp  def solve(x, y):   return jax.lax.linalg.triangular_solve(x, y, left_side=True)  x = jnp.array([[1., 1.], [0., 0.]]) y = jnp.array([[1], [1.]])  print(solve(x, y)) # [[-inf] #  [ inf]] print(solve(x[None], y[None])[0]) # [[0.] #  [1.]] I would expect the second output to be identical to the first. This appears to be the root cause of the issue reported in jax-ml/jax#15429

title: Incorrect device pointer usage in multi-GPU XLA implementation for FP8 GEMM scaling factor
author: wenscarl
body: When attempting to run FP8 cublasLt GEMM on multiple GPUs in the Hopper system, you encountered a CUDA illegal memory access (IMA) error. This error can be replicated by executing the provided script(cuda_ima.py) on two GPUs: python cuda_ima.py --d 4096  In the above command, the --d flag specifies the dimension of the GEMM operation. It is worth noting that larger matrix sizes are more likely to trigger the error. The compute-sanitizer has detected that the illegal memory access (IMA) occurs when accessing the scaling factor pointer. The error message provided is as follows: ========= Invalid __global__ read of size 4 bytes =========     at 0x7f8adde55d00 in sm90_xmma_gemm_e5m2e4m3f32_e5m2e4m3f32_f32_tn_n_tilesize128x128x128_warpgroupsize2x1x1_algo2_execute_segment_k_off_kernel__5x_cublas  The scaling factor pointers on 2 GPUs are 0x7f8adda55d00 (device 0)and 0x7f8adde55d00 (device 1) respectively. But cuBlasLt log shows   computeDesc=[       computeType=COMPUTE_32F       scaleType=R_32F       aScalePointer=0x7f8adda55d00 <-- Device 0       bScalePointer=0x7f8adda55d00 <-- Device 0       cScalePointer=0x7f8adde55d00 <-- Device 1       dScalePointer=0x7f8adde55d00 <-- Device 1   ]  where the cScalePointer and dScalePointer are clearly wrong.

title: Dynamic slice with `uint8` index returns incorrect result
author: jakevdp
body: Reported in jax-ml/jax#16836 Here's a minimal repro: import jax.numpy as jnp from jax import lax  arr = jnp.arange(200) i = jnp.uint8(128) print(lax.dynamic_slice(arr, [i], [1])) # [199] I've double checked that this is not hitting any index normalization on the JAX side; I believe the input values are being passed more-or-less directly to the HLO here: https://github.com/google/jax/blob/b11661696cc7005816359a70242886efa785b429/jax/_src/interpreters/mlir.py#L1472-L1473

title: Bad XLA fusion pattern which does not have runtime benefits but doubles the buffer costs.
author: shawnwang18
body: Found a strange fusion pattern generated after multi_output_fusion pass, like below: fused_computation.593 {   param_0.1608 = f32[2048,16000]{1,0} parameter(0)   convert.1770 = bf16[2048,16000]{1,0} convert(param_0.1608)}   bitcast.15867 = bf16[16000,2048]{0,1} bitcast(convert.1770)   ROOT tuple.143 = (bf16[16000,2048]{0,1}, bf16[2048,16000]{1,0}) tuple(bitcast.15867, convert.1770) } param.9 = f32[2048,16000]{1,0} parameter(4), sharding={devices=[4,2]<=[8]} fusion.593 = (bf16[16000,2048]{0,1}, bf16[2048,16000]{1,0}) fusion(param.9), kind=kLoop, calls=fused_computation.593 get-tuple-element.923 = bf16[16000,2048]{0,1} get-tuple-element(fusion.593), index=0 get-tuple-element.924 = bf16[2048,16000]{1,0} get-tuple-element(fusion.593), index=1 all-gather.20 = bf16[16000,8192]{0,1} all-gather(get-tuple-element.923) all-gather.23 = bf16[8192,16000]{1,0} all-gather(get-tuple-element.924)  Seems that fused_computation.593 does not fuse anything, it does not show any benefits but costs to me, just doubling the buffer cost (fusion.593 needs 2 buffers for outputs). Did some triage, the original HLO is like below: param.9 = f32[2048,16000]{1,0} parameter(4), sharding={devices=[4,2]<=[8]} convert.331 = bf16[2048,16000]{1,0} convert(param.9) bitcast.2749 = bf16[16000,2048]{0,1} bitcast(convert.331) all-gather.20 = bf16[16000,8192]{0,1} all-gather(bitcast.2749) all-gather.23 = bf16[8192,16000]{1,0} all-gather(convert.331)  Then during GPU vertical fusion pass,  the pattern is fused into: fused_computation.593 {   param_0.1608 = f32[2048,16000]{1,0} parameter(0)   convert.1770 = bf16[2048,16000]{1,0} convert(param_0.1608)   ROOT bitcast.15867 = bf16[16000,2048]{0,1} bitcast(convert.1770) } param.9 = f32[2048,16000]{1,0} parameter(4), sharding={devices=[4,2]<=[8]} fusion.593 = bf16[16000,2048]{0,1} fusion(param.9), kind=kLoop, calls=fused_computation.593 all-gather.20 = bf16[16000,8192]{0,1} all-gather(fusion.593) convert.331 = bf16[2048,16000]{1,0} convert(param.9) all-gather.23 = bf16[8192,16000]{1,0} all-gather(convert.331)  i.e, convert.331 is duplicated during vertical fusion pass, and then multiple output fusion pass tries to do multi-output fusion for fusion..593 and convert.331, which create the final strange fusion pattern. Any idea to optimize this fusion pattern?  Current result doubles the memory costs. It looks like the fusion pattern (convert.331 + bitcast) made by vertical fusion pass does not make sense, because fusing bitcast does not actually fuse more computations. title: [Epic] Add command buffer abstraction to XLA:GPU
author: ezhulenev
body: In XLA command buffer is a special kind of callable which has an attached computation regions that at run time will be recorded into "bundle of work" to be submitted for execution. We'll be targeting CUDA graphs (HIP graphs) initially. Example: %Cmd is a command buffer computation %Add (a: s32[], b: s32[]) -> s32[] {   %a = s32[] parameter(0)   %b = s32[] parameter(1)   ROOT %add = s32[] add(s32[] %a, s32[] %b) }  %Multiply (a: s32[], b: s32[]) -> s32[] {   %a = s32[] parameter(0)   %b = s32[] parameter(1)   ROOT %add = s32[] multiply(s32[] %a, s32[] %b) }  %Cmd (a: s32[], b: s32[]) -> s32[] {   %a = s32[] parameter(0)   %b = s32[] parameter(1)   %add = s32[] fusion(s32[] %a, s32[] %b), kind=kLoop, calls=%Add   %mul = s32[] fusion(s32[] %add, s32[] %b.1), kind=kLoop, calls=%Multiply   ROOT %add.1 s32[] fusion(s32[] %add, s32[] %mul), kind=kLoop, calls=%Add }  ENTRY %main (a: s32[], b: s32[]) -> s32[] {   %a = s32[] parameter(0)   %b = s32[] parameter(1)   ROOT %cmd = s32[] command_buffer(s32[] %a, s32[] %b), calls=%Cmd }  ### Tasks - [ ] https://github.com/openxla/xla/issues/5756 - [ ] https://github.com/openxla/xla/issues/5857 - [ ] https://github.com/openxla/xla/issues/5889 - [ ] https://github.com/openxla/xla/issues/6083 - [ ] https://github.com/openxla/xla/issues/6542 - [ ] https://github.com/openxla/xla/issues/6667 - [ ] https://github.com/openxla/xla/issues/6669

title: [xla:gpu] Add experimental CommandBufferScheduling pass to XLA:GPU pipeline
author: ezhulenev
body: Similar to graph_outlining_pass in current XLA:GPU runtime we need a new HLO pass that will outline regions of operations supported by command buffers (right now only fusions) into command buffer regions: Example: %Add (a: s32[], b: s32[]) -> s32[] {   %a = s32[] parameter(0)   %b = s32[] parameter(1)   ROOT %add = s32[] add(s32[] %a, s32[] %b) }  %Multiply (a: s32[], b: s32[]) -> s32[] {   %a = s32[] parameter(0)   %b = s32[] parameter(1)   ROOT %add = s32[] multiply(s32[] %a, s32[] %b) }  %Cmd (a: s32[], b: s32[]) -> s32[] {   %a = s32[] parameter(0)   %b = s32[] parameter(1)   %add = s32[] fusion(s32[] %a, s32[] %b), kind=kLoop, calls=%Add   %mul = s32[] fusion(s32[] %add, s32[] %b.1), kind=kLoop, calls=%Multiply   ROOT %add.1 s32[] fusion(s32[] %add, s32[] %mul), kind=kLoop, calls=%Add }  ENTRY %main (a: s32[], b: s32[]) -> s32[] {   %a = s32[] parameter(0)   %b = s32[] parameter(1)   ROOT %cmd = s32[] command_buffer(s32[] %a, s32[] %b), calls=%Cmd }  We currently do not have a command_buffer HLO operation, so we'll start with a kCall op code with an attached HLO computation. We'll consider graduating custom call to a first class operation later.

title: [xla:gpu] Make command buffers explicit in HLO
author: anlunx
body: Currently the CommandBufferScheduling pass outlines instructions to HloComputation, and calls to command buffers are kCall instructions. We want to be able to distinguish command buffer calls from regular call instructions. This could be achieved through the introduction of a specialized kCallCommandBuffer instruction, a specialized HloComputation representing a command buffer, or potentially a combination of both.

title: [xla:gpu] SPMD pass is not partition aware for reduce op
author: wenscarl
body: SPMD pass is not partition-aware for reduce op. This creates a perf impact in FP8 cases.  o give a example, the operand of reduce has some specific partition specification, e,g. replicated. When the tensor is operated upon, all devices will perform the same computations on the entire tensor, which is not the most efficient. Instead, it's more beneficial to include a combination of slicing and all-reduction operations to complete the task.  A simple reproducer could be: """Tests for the fp8 layers with partitioning.""" from __future__ import absolute_import from __future__ import division from __future__ import print_function  import numpy as np import argparse import optax  import jax import jax.numpy as jnp from jax import random  from flax import linen as nn  # Sharding related from jax.experimental.pjit import pjit from jax.sharding import Mesh from jax.experimental import mesh_utils from flax import linen as nn from flax.linen import spmd # Flax Linen SPMD. from typing import (Iterable, Tuple) from typing import Iterable, Tuple from flax.linen import partitioning as nn_partitioning param_with_axes = nn_partitioning.param_with_axes from flax.training import train_state  # Type annotations Array = jnp.ndarray Dtype = jnp.dtype PRNGKey = jnp.ndarray Shape = Iterable[int]   def _normalize_axes(axes: Iterable[int], ndim: int) -> Tuple[int]:   # A tuple by convention. len(axes_tuple) then also gives the rank efficiently.   return tuple([ax if ax >= 0 else ndim + ax for ax in axes])  def _canonicalize_tuple(x):   if isinstance(x, Iterable):     return tuple(x)   else:     return (x,)   parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description='Benchmark a basic encoder layer') parser.add_argument('--d', type=int, help='matrix dim') args = parser.parse_args()  dim = args.d  class DenseGeneral(nn.DenseGeneral):   kernel_axes: Tuple[str, ...] = ()   bias_axes: Tuple[str, ...] = ()    @nn.compact   def __call__(self, inputs: Array) -> Array:     original_shape = inputs.shape     assert len(original_shape) >= 2      features = _canonicalize_tuple(self.features)     axis = _canonicalize_tuple(self.axis)      inputs = jnp.asarray(inputs, self.dtype)     axis = _normalize_axes(axis, inputs.ndim)      kernel_param_shape = (np.prod([inputs.shape[ax] for ax in axis]),                           np.prod(features))      kernel = param_with_axes(         'kernel',         self.kernel_init,         kernel_param_shape,         self.param_dtype,         axes=self.kernel_axes)     kernel = jnp.asarray(kernel, self.dtype)      if self.use_bias:       bias = param_with_axes(           'bias',           self.bias_init,           (np.prod(features),),           self.param_dtype,           axes=self.bias_axes)       bias = jnp.asarray(bias, self.dtype)     else:       bias = None      inputs, kernel, bias = nn.dtypes.promote_dtype(inputs, kernel, bias,                                                    dtype=self.dtype)      inputs = jnp.reshape(inputs, (-1, np.prod([inputs.shape[ax] for ax in axis])))     if self.dot_general_cls is not None:       dot_general = self.dot_general_cls()     else:       dot_general = self.dot_general      out = dot_general(         inputs,         kernel,         ((axis, 0), ((), ())),         precision=self.precision,     )      # Reshape back the outputs.     out = jnp.reshape(out, (*original_shape[0:-len(axis)], *tuple(features)))      return out   def run():   rules = (('hidden', 'model'),)   device_mesh = mesh_utils.create_device_mesh((2, 2))   mesh = Mesh(devices=device_mesh, axis_names=('data', 'model'))    model = DenseGeneral(dim , kernel_axes=('hidden', 'mlp'), dot_general_cls=nn.Fp8DenseGeneralOp, dtype=jnp.float16)    x = random.normal(random.PRNGKey(0), (dim, dim ), dtype=jnp.float16)   k = random.PRNGKey(0)    spmd.set_logical_axis_rules(rules)    initialized_vars = model.init(k, x)   opt = optax.adam(learning_rate=0.1)   ts_args = {'tx': opt, 'apply_fn': model.apply}   ts_args['params'] = initialized_vars   state = train_state.TrainState.create(**ts_args)    def step_fn(state, x):     def loss_fn(vars, x):       x = spmd.with_logical_constraint(x, ('batch', 'embed'))       y = state.apply_fn(vars, x)       loss = y       return jnp.sum(loss)     grad_fn = jax.value_and_grad(loss_fn, argnums=[0,1])     loss, grads = grad_fn(state.params, x)     state = state.apply_gradients(grads=grads[0])     return state, loss    pjit_step_fn = pjit(       step_fn   )   warmup_iters = 20    with mesh:     # Warmup runs     for _ in range(warmup_iters):       state, loss = pjit_step_fn(state, x)    return loss  print(run()) Note: To run the reproducer, latest FLAX is necessary. cc @kaixih @reedwm @jurahul @philipphack @nouiz

title: FP8 GEMM for the fprop should use fast accumulation
author: kaixih
body: In the current implementation of fp8 gemm, the CUBLASLT_MATMUL_DESC_FAST_ACCUM (link) setting is not configured. This means it defaults to disabled fast accumulation. However, following the transformer engine recipe, it is recommended to enable fast accumulation during the fprop pass, which can further enhance the speed of the fp8 gemm operation. Determining whether the gemm/dot op node in the hlo graph belongs to fprop or bprop poses a non-trivial challenge. In practice, e4m3 is typically used for the fprop gemm, while a combination of e4m3 and e5m2 is used for the bprop gemm. To address this, we propose a solution: if both input data types are e4m3, we will set the aforementioned flag to ensure fast accumulation is utilized specifically during the fprop pass. If this proposal is accepted, we can proceed with preparing a pull request (PR) to implement this change. cc. @reedwm @philipphack @nluehr @instinct79

title: [xla:gpu] Emit thunks directly from HLO
author: anlunx
body: Currently we convert HLO to LMHLO before emitting thunks, and thunks are emitted from the LMHLO. Per runtime roadmap https://docs.google.com/document/d/1XHzJyfq-ZFn9WHoKe4o_urnwS991dFHgWoNRboBK_3I/edit, we will remove the LMHLO, so we need to emit thunks directly from HLO. ThunkEmitter was responsible for generating thunks from HLO, but was gradually removed by a series of PRs, the last one being c8b89b0.  We should bring it back the same way by generating certain type of thunks with it and gradually using it to replace the LMHLO emitter completely.

title: [xla:gpu] Emit CommandBufferThunk
author: anlunx
body: IrEmitterUnnested should emit CommandBufferThunk from a call to command buffer. It should emit the thunk using pure HLO because we don't emit LMHLO for command buffers (In LMHLO the command buffer call is a dummy node that doesn't encode the semantics).

title: [Question][SPMD] All the params in HLO are fused into one and sharding is changed to replicated.
author: baoleai
body: Hi, when I use SPMD, I noticed that on the large model, the last optimized HLO graph is different from the previous ones (there is total 4 optimized hlos). The previous ones were like, constant_5246 = s32[32]{0} constant({...})   param.5 = s64[] parameter(243), sharding={replicated}   param.4 = s64[2,2048]{1,0} parameter(242), sharding={devices=[4,1]0,1,2,3, last_tile_dim_replicate}  but the last one is. param = (f32[], s64[], s64[8,2048]{1,0}, s64[], sharding=={{replicated}, {replicated}, {replicated}}...}  All params have been merged into one, and all sharding spec have been changed to "replicated".  This phenomenon only occurs in large models.

title: Float16 to Float32 conversion crashing with symbols not found: __extendhfsf2 in virualized env
author: milot-mirdita
body: I maintain ColabFold, which internally uses AlphaFold2 (implemented in jax) for predicting protein structures. I have two users running into issues with a crash in xla_client that tries to use __extendhfsf2 for float16 conversion: As far as I can tell the crash should be coming from here: https://github.com/steineggerlab/alphafold/blob/73861947f8a8ffd2d43ffd142c282c7dbd42b4c2/alphafold/model/model.py#L152 The first user (sokrypton/ColabFold#467) was trying to run ColabFold within VirtualBox, which does not seem to have F16C support (https://www.virtualbox.org/ticket/15471). I guess that's why its trying to fall back to the non-native instruction that is not linked into jaxlib. The second user (private communication) is trying to run ColabFold within Docker for Mac in a virtualized environment on an ARM Mac (with an x86_64 image). The emulator also doesn't seem to implement native half conversion instructions and crashes: 2023-11-03 18:36:59.953527: W tensorflow/tsl/platform/profile_utils/cpu_utils.cc:118] Failed to find bogomips or clock in /proc/cpuinfo; cannot determine CPU frequency 2023-11-03 18:37:13.573573: E external/xla/xla/service/cpu/simple_orc_jit.cc:218] Unable to resolve runtime symbol: `__extendhfsf2'. Hint: if the symbol a custom call target, make sure you've registered it with the JIT using XLA_CPU_REGISTER_CUSTOM_CALL_TARGET. JIT session error: Symbols not found: [ __extendhfsf2 ]   Seems like this file:                xla/xla/service/cpu/runtime_fp16.h                    Line 43       in       e112bac                                                 // Converts an F64 value to a F16.                     needs to explicitly handle __extendhfsf2 (instead or in addition to) __gnu_h2f_ieee. I was unsure if I should report this to the jax or xla issue tracker, but this seems more relevant to xla.

title: [xla:gpu] Add efficient command buffer updates
author: ezhulenev
body: Today command buffer sequence always updates command buffer with new commands, which can be very inefficient (*). We need to update only commands that have changes, which in CommandBufferCmd in practice means that buffer allocation address changed. We need something like this: class CommandBufferCmd {   virtual absl::Span<const BufferAllocation::Slice> slices(); };  CommandBufferCmdSequence + CommandBufferThunk should detect if no buffer addresses changes, then there is no need to Update/Record command buffer. The next step would be to detect which buffer slices changed address, and which commands require update, however it's not clear how critical is that for performance, as in practice likely majority of commands will need an update, and the cost of extra tracking can be too expensive. We need to collect some statistics first to decide if it's worth pursuing at all. (*) https://github.com/openxla/xla/blob/main/xla/service/gpu/runtime3/command_buffer_cmd.cc#L57-L67

title: Dumped Modules Names - jit__unnamed_wrapped_function_
author: gobbleturk
body: The module names created via e.g. os.environ["XLA_FLAGS"]="--xla_dump_to" can be  jit__unnamed_wrapped_function_, making them difficult to identify for downstream tasks. In particular if a function is wrapped in a lambda via functools.partial before compiling its dumped name will be jit__unnamed_wrapped_function_ Minimal Repro: import jax.numpy as jnp import jax import os import functools  os.environ["XLA_FLAGS"]="--xla_dump_to=/tmp/hlo_dumps/test_name_4"  def f(b, A):     return jnp.dot(A, A)       b = None h = functools.partial(f, b) jit_h = jax.jit(h)  A = jnp.zeros((5,5)) out = jit_h(A)  Is there a way to retain a meaningful name in this case?

title: XLA dump is not formatted properly with LIBTPU_INIT_ARGS (tested only on cloud)
author: gobbleturk
body: When using the LIBTPU_INIT_ARGS, the XLA dump is not formatted consistently. E.g. if we specify export LIBTPU_INIT_ARGS="--xla_enable_async_all_gather=true", there are these two lines in the tpu_comp_env file: // xla_enable_async_all_gather in the current tpu_comp_env has a non-default value. Default flag value: auto xla_enable_async_all_gather ENABLED  The first comment line breaks a downstream task of using hybrid Sim, but the second line is also missing a colon (also breaking Hybrid Sim) and should probably instead read xla_enable_async_all_gather: ENABLED  Here is a minimal repro import jax import os  os.environ["LIBTPU_INIT_ARGS"] = "--xla_enable_async_all_gather=true" os.environ["XLA_FLAGS"]="--xla_dump_to=/tmp/hlo_dump"  def f(A):     A = jax.numpy.dot(A, A)      return A  A = jax.numpy.zeros((5,5)) jit_f = jax.jit(f) out = jit_f(A)  Alternatively the same bug occurs by setting LIBTPU_INIT_ARGS via an export instead of with python's os.environ, e.g. export LIBTPU_INIT_ARGS="--xla_enable_async_all_gather=true"

title: Nondeterminism in triton-autotuner and others leads to hangs in multi-process gpu execution
author: trevor-m
body: Opening an issue to help us keep track of this even though the discussion has already been ongoing elsewhere. When using multi-process execution, XLA compiles each module indepedently for each process. Nondeterministic passes like triton-autotuner can produce different results per process, which can lead to different optimizations happening later down the pipeline. If any of those optimizations leads to a different ordering of collectives in the schedule, or a different is_async designation for collectives, then there will be deadlocks on the first execution. The ideal solution would be to compile the module once and broadcast the result to all other processes. I believe @hawkinsp is currently planning to work on this.

title: Random generation through threefry2x32 kernel takes too much memory costs in XLA
author: shawnwang18
body: It seems that Jax's default random number generation algorithm threefry2x32 consumes large amout of memory. From search results, the requirement of threefry2x32 is:   To generate random values using threefry2x32 directly, you need to provide a counter array and a PRNG key. The counter array determines the shape of the output, while the PRNG key determines the specific random values generated   The counter and key are arrays of unsigned 32-bit integers. For threefry2x32, both the counter and key have 2 elements   This means to generate a random tensor, threefry2x32 requires 2X memory size of the output tensor.  This will result in big issue about memory consumption, especially for embedding tensor, as embedding tensor is already very large, 2X memory consumption is very likely to cause OOM. Can we work on this problem to see how to reduce the memory consumption of threefry2x32 ? An example of HLO dumps is attached. module_0001.jit_init.sm_9.0_gpu_after_optimizations.txt

title: Incorrect boundary behaviour of `igamma`, `igammac`
author: lucascolley
body: x-ref jax-ml/jax#20507 (comment) > import jax > import scipy > scipy.special.gammainc(0, 1) array(1., dtype=float32) > jax.scipy.special.gammainc(0, 1) array(nan, dtype=float32) > scipy.special.gammaincc(0, 0) array(nan, dtype=float32) > jax.scipy.special.gammaincc(0, 0) array(1., dtype=float32) @steppi:  If $(a, x) \rightarrow (0, 1)$ then $\text{gammainc}(a, x) \rightarrow 1.0$. But $$\lim_{(a, x)\rightarrow (0, 0)} \text{gammaincc}(a, x)$$ depends on the order in which the limit is taken. Taking first $x \rightarrow 0$ and leaving $a > 0$ fixed, the limit tends to 1. Taking $a \rightarrow 0$ and leaving $x > 0$ fixed, the limit tends to zero.  @jakevdp:  We could probably address this at the JAX level, but it would come at the cost of adding a couple select statements to every evaluation of gammainc or gammaincc, which currently lower directly to a single call to lax.igamma or lax.igammac respectively. Better I think would be to update the XLA implementations of these functions, which would have to be done upstream in openxla/xla  As per jax-ml/jax#20507 (comment), the problem arises from a historical mistake in cephes, which has been corrected in SciPy see #11151 (comment).

title: [xla:auto_sharding] Question about resharding costs of Reshape strategies
author: Nullkooland
body: Hi OpenXLA community, I have question about the code to generate sharding strategies and compute resharding costs for HLO reshape op. In the code, the reshape sharding strategyoutput_sepc is generated (reshaped) from one of the operand sharding strategy src_strategy_group->strategies[sid]:                xla/xla/hlo/experimental/auto_sharding/auto_sharding.cc                   Lines 1898 to 1901       in       421f4c4                                                 std::optional<HloSharding> output_spec =                                               hlo_sharding_util::ReshapeSharding(                                                   operand->shape(), ins->shape(),                                                   src_strategy_group->strategies[sid].output_sharding);                     Then compute the communication and memory resharding cost:                xla/xla/hlo/experimental/auto_sharding/auto_sharding.cc                   Lines 1917 to 1923       in       421f4c4                                                 std::vector<double> communication_resharding_costs =                                               CommunicationReshardingCostVector(                                                   src_strategy_group, operand->shape(),                                                   src_strategy_group->strategies[sid].output_sharding, cluster_env);                                           std::vector<double> memory_resharding_costs = MemoryReshardingCostVector(                                               src_strategy_group, operand->shape(),                                               src_strategy_group->strategies[sid].output_sharding, cluster_env);                     It looks like the resharding costs computed are between all operand sharding strategies src_strategy_group and one operand strategy that output_spec reshaped from src_strategy_group->strategies[sid]. I guess this is why I got ZERO resharding cost on a reshape where a all_gather CC OP is actually required. %5 = stablehlo.add %4, %cst_0 {mhlo.sharding = "{devices=[2,4,1,1]0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7}", result_layout = dense<[3, 1, 2, 0]> : tensor<4xindex>, xla_shape = "f16[32,16,1000,256]{3,1,2,0}"} : tensor<32x16x1000x256xf16> %6 = stablehlo.reshape %5 {mhlo.sharding = "{devices=[2,1,1,4]0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 last_tile_dim_replicate}"} : (tensor<32x16x1000x256xf16>) -> tensor<512x1000x256xf16> If my understanding of the Alpa algorithm is correct, the resharding cost should be computed like:  std::vector<double> communication_resharding_costs =  CommunicationReshardingCostVector(       src_strategy_group, operand->shape(),       /* required_sharding */ output_spec, cluster_env);   std::vector<double> memory_resharding_costs = MemoryReshardingCostVector(       src_strategy_group, operand->shape(),       /* required_sharding */ output_spec, cluster_env);

title: Porting XLA to different backends.
author: abhaskumarsinha
body: Hello, I'm very new to the XLA project, so pardon my ignorance here. I'm trying to learn more about the project, optimizations, and their interactions with the hardware. The code everywhere seems well-written and properly documented. The project seems very vast that has been maintained through the effort of tremendous volunteers and not so easy to debug language like Python, so it's very easy to get lost. Here's what I've been able to gather about the project. The DL frameworks seem to construct graphs of their Deep Learning model prior to the computation, where these graphs with their tensor computations get optimized by XLA-like tools called - Linear Algebra Compilers. Now, XLA uses HLO to perform such optimizations to produce latent computational information which is executed by CPU/GPU/TPU into their desired computational formats.  My goal here was to learn how backends of such can be ported swiftly to here are some of my learnings:  The whole project depends upon the ecosystem of LLVM compilers. The LLVM Compilers need to be set and XLA::Compiler and XLA::CPUCompiler, XLA::GPUCompiler needs to be re-written accordingly according to the target platform. These correspond to the files here: xla\service\compiler.h, xla\service\cpu\cpu_compiler.h and similarly for GPU/TPU. In case, if someone fails to port LLVM and LLVM libraries, then things get ugly. All all the four header files mentioned here would require porting, knowing, executor contains stream.h and stream_executor_pimpl.h.  Right?  Also in case, please clarify do they need to ONLY adapt these header files into their new hardware (which doesn't seems so) OR other header files that have been additionally included into those header files too? (that'd be a bit of effort!). For example - if I manage to get LLVM into specific target hardware and now I seek to port my code into that particular hardware, to get that, do I need to ONLY start porting xla\service\compiler.h, xla\service\cpu\cpu_compiler.h OR every header file that has been included in those headers? (which amounts to 18+16 = 34 header files in total in number?)  In case there is any error in understanding the concept, or any disparity in my explanation do please point that out. Best Regards, Abhas Kumar Sinha

title: MHLO Extraction from XLA Compiler
author: Lerisia
body: Hello, I have been delving into the XLA project recently and have a few inquiries regarding accessing MHLO from the XLA compiler. The XLA compiler exhibits a broad array of optimization items, and I am keen on incorporating them into my backend compiler, which is designed for specialized hardware. Given that my compiler is built on MLIR, gaining access to MHLO from the XLA compiler would be highly beneficial. However, it appears that the XLA compiler lacks an exit point for this. As such, I have two questions:  As of the current state, is there a method to access intermediate results in the form of MHLO? Are there plans in the pipeline to offer an interface that allows for obtaining results in the form of MHLO or LMHLO?  I believe it would be great if such plans were to be initiated. This would enable us to deploy the XLA compiler's optimization items in our backend compiler and hardware in the future. Best Regards, Jaeyeon Kim

title: Compiling scatter results in very slow while-loop on TPU
author: j-towns
body: Original JAX issue: jax-ml/jax#21367. I'm using Python version: 3.12.1., jaxlib version: 0.4.28, running on a TPU v4-8 VM. In my use case I need to do batches of dynamic_update_slice operations, and have been using JAX's vmap for that, but was getting extremely slow runtimes (between 10 and 50x slower than expected). I profiled the code and found that the vmapped dynamic_update_slice, which I expected to be doing a scatter, was actually doing a while-loop of dynamic_update_slice ops, looping over the batch axis. I think this while-loop may be preventing parallelization, and causing the very slow runtimes. This JAX code demonstrates the slow-down by comparing the vmapped dynamic_update_slice, which lowers to a single scatter, with an equivalent unrolled Python loop of dynamic_update_slices: from timeit import timeit  from jax import jit, lax, vmap, make_jaxpr import jax.numpy as jnp   # For f which outputs a single array, this simulates vmap using Python map pymap = lambda f: lambda *args: jnp.stack(list(map(f, *args)))  operands = jnp.ones((100, 32)) updates = jnp.ones((100, 2)) starts = jnp.ones((100, 1), dtype='int32')  f = lax.dynamic_update_slice  f_vmapped = jit(vmap(f)) f_pymapped = jit(pymap(f))  # Ensure compiled f_vmapped(operands, updates, starts) f_pymapped(operands, updates, starts)  t_vmapped = timeit(     lambda: f_vmapped(operands, updates, starts).block_until_ready(), number=100 ) / 100  t_pymapped = timeit(     lambda: f_pymapped(operands, updates, starts).block_until_ready(), number=100 ) / 100  print(f"Time vmap(f): {t_vmapped:.2}s") print(f"Time pymap(f): {t_pymapped:.2}s") Running it on a TPU v4-8 VM I get: Time vmap(f): 0.00088s Time pymap(f): 0.00036s  So, to be clear, what I think could be happening is that the unrolled Python loop is faster than scatter because it can be parallelized (the loop iterations have no dependence on each other), whereas the scatter is (for some reason) compiling to a while-loop which cannot be parallelized. The lowered StableHLO of f_vmapped does contain a scatter and no loop, as expected. Removing it solves the bug.   out = out + jnp.dot(jnp.dot(diff, jnp.zeros((dim, dim))), diff)   return out  def mean_fun(x):   outs = jax.vmap(lambda yy: fun(x, yy))(ys)   return jnp.mean(outs)  jitted_grad = jax.jit(jax.grad(mean_fun))(x) grad = jax.grad(mean_fun)(x) print(f'Difference grads: {grad-jitted_grad}') print(f'All close: {jnp.sum(jnp.abs(grad-jitted_grad)) < 1e-3}') # Difference grads: [ 0.        -1.0000002 -2.0000007] # All close: False  If working correctly, it should print: Difference grads: [0. 0. 0.] All close: True  I bisected the problem to XLA commit: 0dc5563 @jmaksymc HLO dumps from that commit (bad) and the immediately preceding commit (good): dumps.tgz We should either fix or revert that commit.

title: ReduceScatterCreator - Misses One Pattern
author: patrick-toulme
body: The xla::gpu::ReduceScatterCreator pass misses one small pattern. It misses the case where the constant pool is  slice size * num_replica groups up to full tensor size. Example: Constant pool: {0,0,0,0,...128,128,128,128...256,256,256}  Example pool generation: std::vector<int32_t> repeated_pool;   repeated_pool.reserve(replica_ids_size * num_replica_groups);     for (int32_t idx = 0; idx < replica_ids_size; ++idx) {     for (size_t group_idx = 0; group_idx < num_replica_groups; ++group_idx) {       repeated_pool.push_back(idx * sinfo.size);     }   }

title: How to use PJRT C API v.2
author: janpfeifer
body: hi, I'm forking the previous #7038 because that seems to get PJRT to work leveraging the C++ wrappers. I'm trying to build a PJRT wrap for Go leveraging purely the PJRT C API to power an ML framework for Go (I've written here before so some may be familiar with the project. But hopefully the questions are generic for anyone building an ML for any X language (or anyone else needing compiled accelerator code). Question 1 and the most important (before I spend too much time on it): is using simply the pjrt_c_api.h file, doing a dlopen on the compiled plugins (from openxla/xla for now), and using it directly a valid approach ? Or does one need any of the helper/wrappers around it under xla/xla/pjrt ?  Are there specific considerations or limitations one should be aware of when taking this path? For the time being in the GoMLX project I'll use XlaBuilder to generate the StableHLO (it provides me shape inference of the result of the ops). But later the goal would be to use purely the PJRT C API, if viable. Question 2: While the pjrt_c_api.h header provides function definitions, there are several aspects that I found unclear and I was wondering if there is additional documentation. Some examples -- apologies if noob questions, but I usually don't interact at this level:  What are the available extension types and their purpose ? Are there documentation on the CPU/GPU plugins (from OpenXLA/XLA repository) ? Client/Multi-Node Semantics: How are PjRT clients and multi-node setups related? If there are multiple GPUs on a machine, should one client be created per GPU instance? Is this behavior consistent across different plugins? Buffer Abstractions: What are the underlying abstractions for PjRT buffers? What synchronization mechanisms are in place (host-device, cross-device, cross-plugin)? How does the concept of tiling (mentioned in pjrt_c_api.h) work?  Are there any design documents or references (perhaps from JAX or TensorFlow) that would be helpful in understanding these aspects of the C API? Btw, since I'm opening the issue, one potential (C vs C++) issue with pjrt_c_api.h: on line 56 whenever I include it on the most trivial C file, the compile fails with: ./pjrt_c_api.h:56:3: error: unknown type name 'PJRT_Extension_Base'  Seems simple, it's missing a struct because struct PJRT_Extension_Base is not aliased with a typedef yet, it only happens 2 lines below. It does compile in C++ though. Maybe I'm missing some compilation flag  for C? (I tried both gcc and clang, both reported the same error). typedef struct PJRT_Extension_Base {   size_t struct_size;   PJRT_Extension_Type type;   PJRT_Extension_Base* next;   // <-- line with error. } PJRT_Extension_Base; PJRT_DEFINE_STRUCT_TRAITS(PJRT_Extension_Base, next); Thanks in advance for any answers and/or pointers! :) ps.: If I manage to get the PJRT C API to work nicely, I would be happy to contribute with documentation (perhaps a tutorial) on how to use PJRT C API for consumers (as opposed to hardware developers) that is generic to help others.

/usr/local/lib/python3.10/dist-packages/jax_plugins/xla_cuda12/xla_cuda_plugin.so #6  0x00007ffeff74c427 in tsl::profiler::ProfilerCollection::CollectData(tensorflow::profiler::XSpace*) ()    from /usr/local/lib/python3.10/dist-packages/jax_plugins/xla_cuda12/xla_cuda_plugin.so #7  0x00007ffeff74bef8 in xla::profiler::PLUGIN_Profiler_CollectData(PLUGIN_Profiler_CollectData_Args*) ()    from unitialized activity_buffers_ here: https://cs.opensource.google/tensorflow/tensorflow/+/master:third_party/xla/xla/backends/profiler/gpu/cupti_collector.cc;drc=17cedabb755224148be9854551d4efd172af10e5;l=630 The activity_buffer will called. But when CUPTI failed to initialize, this function is not called. The library uses an unconstructed object so it leads to a segfault. ### Tasks

title: [XLA:GPU] Check failed in collective_pipeliner when using gradient accumulation with non-unrolled loop
author: qGentry
body: Hi, I have following setup:  Transformer model with N layers scanned over input fully sharded data parallel sharding asynchronous communications (latency-hiding scheduler, pipelined all-gather,all-reduce,reduce-scatter)  I'm using following flags: --xla_gpu_graph_level=0  --xla_gpu_enable_triton_gemm=false  --xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=  --xla_gpu_enable_latency_hiding_scheduler=true  --xla_gpu_enable_all_gather_combine_by_dim=false  --xla_gpu_enable_reduce_scatter_combine_by_dim=false  --xla_gpu_enable_pipelined_all_gather=true  --xla_gpu_enable_pipelined_reduce_scatter=true  --xla_gpu_enable_pipelined_all_reduce=true  --xla_gpu_enable_pipelined_collectives=false  --xla_gpu_enable_while_loop_double_buffering=true  --xla_gpu_enable_highest_priority_async_stream=true  --xla_gpu_disable_async_collectives=collectivebroadcast,alltoall,collectivepermute This works correctly and indeed hide layers' weights all-gather and gradient reduce-scatter behind computations. Problems are starting to arise when I try to use gradient accumulation in this setup. It is implemented like this:     grads_sum = jax.tree_map(jnp.zeros_like, train_state.params)     train_state, grads_sum = jax.lax.fori_loop(         lower=0,         upper=num_minibatches_in_batch,         body_fun=_loop_body,         init_val=(train_state, grads_sum),         unroll=False,     )      mean_grads = jax.tree_map(lambda x: x / num_minibatches_in_batch, grads_sum) When I set gradient accumulation factor (num_minibatches_in_batch in this snippet) to value greater than 1, I'm getting following error during compilation: 2024-07-01 12:57:35.488299: F external/xla/xla/service/collective_pipeliner.cc:675] Check failed: last_cloned != nullptr (0 vs. nullptr)  Here is --xla_dump_to result: xla_dump.tgz One important fact here is that if I set unroll in jax.lax.fori_loop to True, then there is no compilation error and everything works. But this obviously leads to additional memory usage proportional to gradient accumulation factor so this hack doesn't seem to be viable. My hypothesis is that when using --xla_gpu_enable_while_loop_double_buffering=true with pipelined collectives and latency  hiding scheduler, XLA compiler tries to double buffer this fori_loop which is actually undesired behavior. Basically, there are two problems:  Bug in compiler that leads to hard-to-parse source of error in JAX code If my hypothesis is correct, I would like to have mechanism to disable while_loop_double_buffering for specific loops (like gradient accumulation loop) or enable only for specific loops (like layers loop)  I've tested this on JAX 0.4.29 and 0.4.30.

title: [XLA:GPU] Fine-grained remat policy makes async/pipelined collectives execute in the main stream
author: qGentry
body: Description Hi, I have following setup:  Transformer model with N layers scanned over input fully sharded data parallel sharding asynchronous communications (latency-hiding scheduler, pipelined all-gather,all-reduce,reduce-scatter)  I'm using following flags: --xla_gpu_graph_level=0  --xla_gpu_enable_latency_hiding_scheduler=true  --xla_gpu_enable_all_gather_combine_by_dim=false  --xla_gpu_enable_reduce_scatter_combine_by_dim=false  --xla_gpu_enable_pipelined_all_gather=true  --xla_gpu_enable_pipelined_reduce_scatter=true  --xla_gpu_enable_pipelined_all_reduce=true  --xla_gpu_enable_pipelined_collectives=false  --xla_gpu_enable_while_loop_double_buffering=true  --xla_gpu_enable_highest_priority_async_stream=true  --xla_gpu_all_reduce_combine_threshold_bytes=2147483648  --xla_gpu_all_gather_combine_threshold_bytes=2147483648   --xla_gpu_reduce_scatter_combine_threshold_bytes=2147483648 --xla_gpu_disable_async_collectives=collectivebroadcast,alltoall,collectivepermute To speedup backward by fine-grained reduction of activations recomputation, I marked each dense layer's output in transformer block with specific name: result = jax.lax.dot_general(     inputs,     kernel,     dimension_numbers=((axis, contract_ind), ((), ())),     precision=self.precision,     preferred_element_type=self.accumulator_dtype, ) result = jax.ad_checkpoint.checkpoint_name(result, self.activation_dot_name)  So, for example, in attention layer I have "dot_attention_query", "dot_attention_key", "dot_attention_value", "dot_attention_out". And then I apply checkpoint policy on scanned function which accepts list of activation names to checkpoint: def rematted_layer(layer):     return nn.remat(         layer,         policy=jax.checkpoint_policies.save_only_these_names(             *self.config.save_names_for_bwd         ),         prevent_cse=not self.config.scan,     )  and then scan It over embeddings: apply_block = rematted_layer(apply_block) apply_block = nn.scan(     apply_block,     length=self.config.num_layers,     variable_axes={         "params": 0,     },     variable_broadcast=False,     split_rngs={"params": True},     metadata_params={nn.PARTITION_NAME: "layers"}, ) block = TransformerBlock(     name="scan",     config=self.config.block, ) embeddings, _ = apply_block(block, embeddings, None)  If I set self.config.save_names_for_bwd to empty list (which is basically equivalent to "nothing_saveable" policy), then communications works correctly - all-gather/reduce-scatters/all-reduces are overlapped with computations, as can be seen on this perfetto trace:  nothing_saveable.tgz But as soon as I start to specify some names in self.config.save_names_for_bwd, for example,     save_names_for_bwd:       - dot_mlp_out       - dot_attention_value       - dot_attention_query       - dot_attention_key While these activations is indeed not recomputed during backward pass, all communications are executed in main stream without any overlapping with computations:  save_only_these_names_trace.tgz System info (python version, jaxlib version, accelerator, etc.) >>> import jax; title: Marking a CUDA custom call as command buffer-compatible has no effect
author: andportnoy
body: This seems to happen because this piece of logic only looks at registrations for generic platform gpu:                xla/xla/service/gpu/command_buffer_scheduling.cc                   Lines 162 to 165       in       5e9ce97                                                 auto registration = ffi::FindHandler(hlo->custom_call_target(), "gpu");                                           return registration.ok()                                                      ? ffi::IsCommandBufferCompatible(registration->traits)                                                      : false;                     Hence custom calls registered for CUDA are not taken into account. @ezhulenev has suggested offline that the fix might be to do platform name canonicalization more thoroughly. A quick way to repro is to modify the JAX cuda_custom_call test as follows: diff --git a/docs/cuda_custom_call/cuda_custom_call_test.py b/docs/cuda_custom_call/cuda_custom_call_test.py index 563462feb..0e3a5453b 100644 --- a/docs/cuda_custom_call/cuda_custom_call_test.py +++ b/docs/cuda_custom_call/cuda_custom_call_test.py @@ -72,7 +72,8 @@ library = ctypes.cdll.LoadLibrary(SHARED_LIBRARY)  xla_client.register_custom_call_target(name=XLA_CUSTOM_CALL_TARGET_FWD,                                         fn=ffi.pycapsule(library.FooFwd),                                         platform=XLA_PLATFORM, -                                       api_version=XLA_CUSTOM_CALL_API_VERSION) +                                       api_version=XLA_CUSTOM_CALL_API_VERSION, +                                       traits=1)    # our forward primitive will also return the intermediate output b+1 @@ -111,7 +112,8 @@ mlir.register_lowering(foo_fwd_p, _foo_fwd_lowering, platform=JAX_PLATFORM)  xla_client.register_custom_call_target(name=XLA_CUSTOM_CALL_TARGET_BWD,                                         fn=ffi.pycapsule(library.FooBwd),                                         platform=XLA_PLATFORM, -                                       api_version=XLA_CUSTOM_CALL_API_VERSION) +                                       api_version=XLA_CUSTOM_CALL_API_VERSION, +                                       traits=1)   then run the following script (you'll need Nsight Systems CLI installed), which will show whether each kernel was launched as part of a CUDA graph or not: XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_graph_min_graph_size=1 nsys profile --cuda-graph-trace=node -o custom-call-graph --force-overwrite=true python cuda_custom_call_test.py nsys stats -r cuda_kern_exec_trace --force-export=true custom-call-graph.nsys-rep

title: StableHLO spec has signed integers instead of signless, but XLA appears to use signless integers
author: efferifick
body: Hi, I am reading the StableHLO specification. The EBNF-like grammar shown in the Types / Element Type subsection of the StableHLO spec IntegerType ::= SignedIntegerType | UnsignedIntegerType SignedIntegerType ::= 'si2' | 'si4' | 'si8' | 'si16' | 'si32' | 'si64' UnsignedIntegerType ::= 'ui2' | 'ui4' | 'ui8' | 'ui16' | 'ui32' | 'ui64'  and the explanation that follows  Integer types can be either signed (si) or unsigned (ui) and have one of the supported bit widths (2, 4, 8, 16, 32 or 64). Signed siN types represent integer values from -2^(N-1) to 2^(N-1)-1 inclusive, and unsigned uiN types represent integer values from 0 to 2^N-1 inclusive.  state that signed integers are allowed in StableHLO. However, running this handcrafted simple program in XLA via JAX: import jax from jax._src.interpreters import mlir  program = """ func.func @main(%0 : tensor<si64>) -> tensor<si64> {   %1 = "stablehlo.add"(%0, %0) : (tensor<si64>, tensor<si64>) -> tensor<si64>   func.return %1 : tensor<si64> } """ module = mlir.ir.Module.parse(program, context=mlir.make_ir_context()) bytecode = mlir.module_to_bytecode(module) client = jax._src.xla_bridge.backends()["cpu"] loaded = client.compile(bytecode) jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True) a = jax.numpy.array(1, dtype=jax.numpy.int64) print(loaded.execute([a])) Gives me the following error: Traceback (most recent call last):   File "/home/ubuntu/Code/trace/bug.py", line 10, in <module>     module = mlir.ir.Module.parse(program, context=mlir.make_ir_context())              ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ jaxlib.mlir._mlir_libs._site_initialize.<locals>.MLIRError: Unable to parse module assembly: error: "-":3:8: 'stablehlo.add' op operand #0 must be ranked tensor of f8E4M3B11FNUZ type or f8E4M3FN type or f8E4M3FNUZ type or f8E5M2 type or f8E5M2FNUZ type or 16-bit float or 32-bit float or 64-bit float or bfloat16 type or pred (AKA boolean or 1-bit integer) or 4/8/16/32/64-bit signless integer or 4/8/16/32/64-bit unsigned integer or complex type with 32-bit float or 64-bit float elements or 4/8/16/32-bit uniform quantized signed integer or 4/8/16/32-bit uniform quantized unsigned integer or 4/8/16/32-bit uniform quantized per axis signed integer or 4/8/16/32-bit uniform quantized per axis unsigned integer values, but got 'tensor<si64>'  note: "-":3:8: see current operation: %0 = "stablehlo.add"(%arg0, %arg0) : (tensor<si64>, tensor<si64>) -> tensor<si64>  Using signless integers works even though they are not included in the specification. This is a really minor bug, but I wanted to point it out. Maybe this is more of an issue with JAX too?

title: CUDA 12.6 uses PTX ISA version 8.5 not 8.6
author: sclarkson
body: While running JAX compiled with CUDA 12.6, I get error messages to the effect of '+ptx86' is not a recognized feature for this target (ignoring feature)  Per the table here, both CUDA 12.5 and 12.6 use PTX ISA 8.5, making the calculation below no longer correct.                xla/xla/service/gpu/llvm_gpu_backend/gpu_backend_lib.cc                   Lines 302 to 318       in       ce2fffa                                                 int DetermineHighestSupportedPtxVersionFromCudaVersion(                                               stream_executor::ToolVersion cuda_version) {                                             if (cuda_version[0] < 11) {                                               // For everything below CUDA 11 we just fall back to PTX 6.5.                                               // We don't support CUDA below 11 anymore.                                               return kFallbackPtxVersion;                                             }                                                                                        // Mapping determined from                                             // https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/parallel-thread-execution/index.html#release-notes                                             // Examples:                                             // CUDA 11.0 -> PTX 7.0                                             // CUDA 11.1 -> PTX 7.1                                             // CUDA 12.0 -> PTX 8.0                                             // CUDA 12.4 -> PTX 8.4 etc.                                             return (cuda_version[0] - 4) * 10 + cuda_version[1];                                           }

title: Hard error with PGLE Accruracy Checker
author: shraiysh
body: In a recent commit, a hard error was introduced in PGLE when instructions are missing from the profile. The hard error has the following problems:  If there is a conditional operation (if-else) in HLO, and it always jumps to the same branch, then the other computation never gets executed - hence will not have its costs in the profile. If we then use this profile for PGLE, it will crash. There are some modules that only run during initialization. If the profiler runs after a few training steps, then these modules do not run for the profiler. If we then use this profile for PGLE, it will crash.  Possible solutions:  Hard error behind a flag like --strict-pgle. The default behavior should not have a hard error with missing instructions, instead it should use a default cost for them. Discuss a testing methodology that should be able to test the effect of PGLE on HLO schedule so we do not have to have this hard error at all.

title: XLA not fusing reduce for CPU tensor with > 32 elements
author: JeffGreen
body: Hello! As per jax-ml/jax#23427, I'm noticing that XLA on CPU isn't doing a fused reduction sum for a  very simple function if the input tensor is > 32 elements: @jax.jit def func_a(input_tensor):     return jnp.sum(jnp.cos(input_tensor))  n_elem = 32  print("************LOWERED**********") print(jax.jit(func_a).lower(jnp.ones(n_elem, dtype=jnp.float32)).as_text())  print("************COMPILED**********") print(jax.jit(func_a).lower(jnp.ones(n_elem, dtype=jnp.float32)).compile().as_text())  If I run this with n_elem = 32 and then again with n_elem=33, I get the same lowered stablehlo, but different compiled output.  In the case of the tensor with length 32, I see loop fusion: HloModule jit_func_a, is_scheduled=true, entry_computation_layout={(f32[32]{0})->f32[]}, allow_spmd_sharding_propagation_to_parameters={true}, allow_spmd_sharding_propagation_to_output={true}  %region_0.2 (Arg_0.3: f32[], Arg_1.4: f32[]) -> f32[] {   %Arg_0.3 = f32[] parameter(0), metadata={op_name="jit(func_a)/jit(main)/jit(func_a)/reduce_sum"}   %Arg_1.4 = f32[] parameter(1), metadata={op_name="jit(func_a)/jit(main)/jit(func_a)/reduce_sum"}   ROOT %add.5 = f32[] add(f32[] %Arg_0.3, f32[] %Arg_1.4), metadata={op_name="jit(func_a)/jit(main)/jit(func_a)/reduce_sum" source_file="/home/jgreen/gits/learn/python/scratch/jax_reduce_bug.py" source_line=7} }  %fused_computation source_file="/home/jgreen/gits/learn/python/scratch/jax_reduce_bug.py" source_line=7}   %constant.1 = f32[] constant(0)   ROOT %reduce.1 = f32[] reduce(f32[32]{0} %cosine.1, f32[] %constant.1),
